attestation_log.source_title: Chewing gum bezoars of the gastrointestinal tract
attestation_log.author: David E. Milov et al.
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: gum passes through / gum digestive system
attestation_log.exact_quote: "It probably passes through slower than most foodstuffs, but eventually the normal housekeeping waves in the digestive tract will sort of push it through"
attestation_log.evidence: Peer-reviewed paper in Pediatrics (August 1998) by Milov et al. documenting gum bezoar cases. Milov is quoted in Scientific American (2007) and HowStuffWorks using the 'passes through' framing directly. The paper is the foundational clinical source cited by virtually every subsequent debunking article. The quote is attributed to Milov in Scientific American's 2007 article, which drew on the 1998 Pediatrics work.
attestation_log.role_evidence: The 1998 Pediatrics paper by Milov et al. is the earliest identified primary source in which a named medical authority explicitly articulates the 'gum passes through' corrective framing in a citable, widely-reproduced form; all subsequent online debunking articles trace back to this paper and Milov's quotes.
attestation_log.cited_via: HowStuffWorks citation: 'Milov, David E. et al. "Chewing gum bezoars of the gastrointestinal tract." Pediatrics. August 1998.'

lexical.adversarial_notes: Conducted seven distinct web searches targeting: (a) general history/origin of the 'swallowed gum passes through in days' framing; (b) pre-1993 newspaper and book sources using n-grams 'gum passes through,' 'swallowed gum days,' 'gum digestive system,' 'gum comes out'; (c) the Snopes.com reference bibliography for this myth, which is the most authoritative compiled source list; (d) the 1998 Milov et al. Pediatrics paper and its cited references; (e) pre-1993 medical journal literature on swallowed gum; (f) variant phrasings including 'swallow gum few days,' 'passes through digestive system,' and date-restricted queries for 1970–1992. The Snopes reference list — the most comprehensive bibliography for this topic — cites the Minneapolis Star Tribune 'Chew on This for a While' (May 26, 1993, p. T4) as its earliest popular-press source, which is exactly the proposed earliest date, and the LA Times 'Between Chew and Shoe' by Roy Rivenburg (September 19, 1993) as the next. No source in the Snopes bibliography predates May 26, 1993. The 1998 Milov et al. Pediatrics paper cites two pre-1993 medical papers — Cotner M (1992, South Med J 75:775, 'Fecal impaction due to bubble gum bezoar') and Truex JH et al. (1989, Am J Disease Child 143:253-254, 'Bubble gum bezoar') — but both concern pathological complications (bezoar/blockage), not the corrective reassurance framing that gum 'passes through in a few days.' These were ruled out as instances of the target framing. Multiple authoritative sources (McGill OSS, Scientific American, Healthline, Duke Health, Snopes, HowStuffWorks) explicitly state that the origin of the myth-debunking framing is unknown and cannot be traced to any specific earlier source. A 1853 NCBI article about swallowed teeth passing through the alimentary canal was found but ruled out as it concerns teeth, not gum, and predates modern chewing gum entirely. Limitations: Google Books full-text search for pre-1993 books was not directly accessible; Usenet archives (Google Groups) were not directly searchable in this session; paywalled newspaper archives (ProQuest Historical Newspapers, Newspapers.com) could not be accessed. It is possible that an earlier instance exists in an undigitized or paywalled source, but no credible evidence of one was found across all accessible sources.
